__doc__: Where a venue's floor plans sit in the world, so their drawings can be turned
into map geometry.
The frame belongs to the venue, not to a sheet. Every floor of a building is
one drawing issued floor by floor — the convention centre's two put its walls
at the same page coordinates to a tenth of a point — so they share a single
page-to-world transform and cannot drift apart. Fit them separately and two
floors of the same room can disagree about where that room is; sharing the
frame makes that impossible rather than merely small.
`frame.page` is a rectangle in PDF points, y up from the bottom-left corner —
the space plan-labels.py reports and pdf-to-svg.py writes its paths in. Here
it is the whole page, so nothing about the transform depends on a crop.
`frame.bounds` is where that rectangle's corners land: (x0, y0) is the
south-west corner and (x1, y1) the north-east one. The mapping is linear in
Web Mercator, which is what a map draws in, and the plans are drawn to scale
with north up, so a uniform scale and an offset is the whole transform.
`legend` is where a sheet prints its key. Nothing inside is part of the
building, and the swatches are drawn in the same colours as the thing they
stand for, so they have to be excluded by position rather than by colour.
scripts/fit-plan.mjs re-derives the frame against the venue's OpenStreetMap
footprint and reports how closely each sheet then agrees with it.
